Weddington is Charlotte's horse-country suburb — estate lots, pasture, and some of the largest homes in Union County standing on them, under mature oak canopy and along the creek bottoms that web the town. Big houses mean big roof systems: long soffit runs, multiple chimneys, complex junctions where wings and additions meet, and attics measured in thousands of square feet. We survey every structure on the parcel, rank them by activity, and sequence exclusions so each building closes behind the animals' exit, ending with nowhere left indoors. Barns deserve their own read: raccoons in the hay-loft end of a barn are a feed-contamination problem as much as a wildlife one, and the sealing there is metal flashing and hardware cloth fitted to timber framing, not residential trim.

State rules ride along: bat evictions are prohibited during pup season, May 1 through July 31, so Weddington's big attic colonies — little browns and big browns both — are mapped in summer and excluded completely from August, every entry across those long rooflines found and sealed.

At ground level the estate landscape has its own log: groundhog burrows in the pasture fence lines and under outbuildings — a genuine hazard to horses, and treated that way — and mole systems in the irrigated lawns. Ground work is trapped and closed together; an emptied fence-line burrow is screened or collapsed where the ground allows, because groundhogs re-let proven banks quickly.

Stallings.extendedBody:
The repeating floor plan and the repeating entry

A Stallings squirrel job starts with identification: which builder, which model, which roof. Production homes concentrate their wildlife risk in a handful of details — the vinyl soffit corners, the un-screened gable vents, the junction where the porch roof dies into the wall, the garage door's bottom corners. We seal in metal that outlasts the detail's design life and tell you plainly which detail failed, because it will fail the same way on the same model across the street — and because builders' warranty windows make some of these the builder's repair, not yours, if the house is young enough. Either way, the sealed detail ends the pattern at your address.

Licensed agents and the bat calendar

Our Stallings operators are licensed Wildlife Control Agents with the NC Wildlife Resources Commission; removal runs through the state depredation-permit system, the permit for your property forming the job's legal basis. Bats follow North Carolina's hard calendar — no evictions during pup season, May 1 through July 31 — so the big brown colonies in Stallings' older attics are mapped in summer and excluded completely from August. A colony excluded at only its main entry relocates to its second one; the full-entry read is what makes August the last month of the problem.
